newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - UK minister rebuts PFI health critics.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - UK minister rebuts PFI health critics.

text.p: British junior health minister John Horam on Friday hit back at criticism that the government's private finance plans have failed in the health sector, saying he was confident 500 million stg of projects would be delivered by April 1995.
Horam defended his department's record on the flagship private finance initiative (PFI) policy to get private money to build hospitals in an interview with Reuters.
The Department of Health was already close to announcing some major agreements, he said.
"We are confident of getting 500 million stg by April. If we are able to bring in a 170 million stg project and a 30 million one in the next few months then we are almost half way there."
The minister was seeking to implement a damage limitation exercise in face of mounting criticism about PFI health projects before the Conservative Party conference kicks off next week.

One leading NHS (National Health Service) trust adviser, Gordon Best of Kings Fund research told Reuters this week the policy was a "dead duck" in the health sector, and was providing unsuitable projects at higher costs than the health service could afford.
Andrew Neil, head of the NHS PFI unit, also slammed the issue of project suitability.

One construciton industry leader told Reuters "Companies are frustrated with the whole negotiating approach -- I wouldn't say it should be abandoned but the process needs radical surgery." But Horam said the picture was not so bleak and pointed to one example of a government solution to industry worries.
He said that the government had offered private sector companies a guarantee in law that it would pick up residual liabilities if a health trust went bankrupt.
The trusts are responsible for meeting the PFI payments over terms stretching over as long as 30 years.
"This is one reason why these projects have taken so long," said Horam. "We got Royal Asset on this (provision) in June and it makes that committment inescapeable."
Horam also defended the fact that that no major projects have been agreed and started up since PFI was first introduced.
"A great deal has been done. Although the process is slow, everything is still on course. Also you must remember health PFI started later than the prison and motorways."

He also denied there was a crisis of confidence among UK contractors. Some players have told industry leaders that they will not be bidding for any more health projects, saying they are fed up with spending million of pounds on bidding with no results.

Despite reports that big players like John Laing Plc, Tarmac Plc, Alfred McAlpine and Kier Group Plc have pulled out of PFI bid lists, Horam said "The big boys are competing in PFI. No single project has been left without a bidder."
